meta.title: Reranking for Better Answers
meta.thesis: Reranking for Better Answers is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A retriever finds many plausible docs and a reranker must put the truly useful evidence first. By the end, they should be able to build or review reranking experiment with baseline top-k, reranked top-k, and answer quality checks, measure relevant evidence in the top three chunks, and catch the failure where reranking improves average relevance but buries rare edge-case documents.

mentalMap.caption: Use a slower, more precise scorer on a short candidate list so the generator receives stronger evidence.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Reranking improves RAG when recall exists but the best evidence is not reliably high enough to fit into context.

modules.title: Reranking starts after recall
modules.sub: A second stage only helps candidates that already exist.
modules.summary: Reranking is precision work on a candidate set, not magic retrieval.
objectives: Explain first-stage retrieval versus second-stage reranking.
Identify recall failures that reranking cannot fix.
Decide how many candidates to send to a reranker.

blocks.title: Recall first, precision second

spans.text: Problem anchor: a policy assistant retrieves the right cancellation clause at rank 17, but the prompt packs only top 6. The generated answer cites a nearby FAQ instead. A reranker can help because the evidence exists but is badly ordered.
If the cancellation clause never appears in top 40, reranking is the wrong first fix. Look at chunking, filters, embedding model, sparse search, or query rewriting.
For every failed answer, ask “was the needed chunk retrieved anywhere?” before changing the prompt.

blocks.analogy: A reranker can choose the best cards in your hand; it cannot draw a missing card.

blocks.title: Case study: answerable but out of budget

spans.text: In an internal handbook bot, dense retrieval puts “contractor PTO exceptions” at rank 13 behind general PTO policy pages. A cross-encoder reranker scores the query and each candidate together, moving the exception to rank 2.
The answer changes from a generic policy summary to a grounded answer with the exception cited. The improvement came from context selection, not a more verbose prompt.

items.text: Capture the top-40 candidate list for the failing query.
Mark whether the expected source appears.
Rerank the list with a pairwise scorer.
Compare packed top-k before and after reranking.

blocks.title: Reranker fit
blocks.prompt: When is reranking unlikely to help?

options.text: When there are more than five documents in the corpus.
When the decisive evidence is absent from the candidate set.

blocks.explanation: Reranking reorders retrieved candidates; it does not search the whole corpus by itself.

modules.title: Cross-encoders read query and passage together
modules.sub: Precision improves because the scorer sees the pair.
modules.summary: A reranker spends more compute per candidate to judge relevance more carefully.
objectives: Explain why reranking usually happens on tens of candidates, not millions.

blocks.title: Pairwise scoring is the expensive part

spans.text: Embedding retrieval usually encodes the query and passage separately, enabling fast approximate search over many chunks. A cross-encoder-style reranker reads the query and candidate passage together, which gives a richer relevance judgment but costs more per pair.
This is why a common pattern is retrieve 40 or 100 candidates quickly, rerank that short list, then pack the best 5 to 10 into the prompt.
If latency is tight, measure p95 with realistic candidate counts rather than assuming reranking is free.

blocks.analogy: The retriever scans the library catalog; the reranker opens a short stack of books.

blocks.title: Worked sizing: 60 candidates to 8 evidence chunks

spans.text: A product-doc assistant retrieves 60 candidates with hybrid search. The reranker scores each query-passage pair and returns the top 8. The answer prompt receives fewer but sharper chunks.
If p95 latency rises too much, the team can reduce first-stage top-k, cache reranker results for common queries, or route only ambiguous categories through reranking.

items.text: Choose candidate count from recall eval, not a default.
Trim to the context budget used by generation.
Log candidate count, rerank latency, and before/after rank of expected sources.

blocks.title: Architecture tradeoff
blocks.prompt: Why not use a cross-encoder over every chunk in a large KB?

options.text: It is too expensive per query; first-stage retrieval narrows the candidate set.
Vector search is always more accurate than reranking.

blocks.explanation: Rerankers are usually second-stage models because pairwise scoring is costly.

modules.title: Rerank the evidence you can defend
modules.sub: The reranker objective must match answer quality.
modules.summary: Reranking should optimize support for the user question.
objectives: Distinguish topical relevance from answer support.
Use graded judgments for ambiguous passages.
Spot cases where reranking over-favors summaries.

blocks.title: Relevant is not always sufficient

spans.text: A passage can mention “refunds” and rank high while lacking the exact enterprise exception. Reranking should favor the chunk that answers the question, not the chunk that merely shares vocabulary.
When evaluating rerankers, label candidates with grades such as direct support, partial support, background, and irrelevant. This produces better feedback than a binary relevant/not relevant tag.
The best evidence chunk should let a reviewer verify the final sentence without hunting elsewhere.

blocks.analogy: A witness who was in the building is not as useful as one who saw the event.

cells.text: Find passages about the same subject.
Can rank background above answer evidence.
Find passages that prove the requested claim.
Needs better labels and harder evals.
Strong for policy and product docs.

blocks.title: Support vs topic
blocks.prompt: The top reranked chunk is about refunds but lacks the exception asked about. What label should it receive?

options.text: Direct support because it shares the topic.
Partial or background support, not direct answer support.
Irrelevant because all refund pages are useless.

blocks.explanation: Graded labels help rerankers and reviewers distinguish topic overlap from proof.

modules.title: Implement reranking as a replaceable stage
modules.sub: Keep retrieval, reranking, and packing separately testable.
modules.summary: Reranking should be observable plumbing, not hidden prompt magic.
objectives: Preserve original retrieval ranks for debugging.
Predict how a simple scorer changes the packed set.

blocks.title: A reranker is a scoring function over pairs

spans.text: In production the scorer may be a cross-encoder, LLM judge, or hosted reranking API. The interface is simple: given query and candidate text, return a relevance score plus enough metadata to debug.
Spaced recall: from hybrid retrieval, keep original dense and sparse ranks. If reranking hurts exact identifier queries, those ranks help explain why.
Store the candidate text, original rank, rerank score, and final packed rank in traces.

blocks.title: Small rerank harness with trace fields
blocks.code:
def toy_score(query, text):
    q_terms = set(query.lower().split())
    t_terms = set(text.lower().split())
    return len(q_terms & t_terms) / max(1, len(q_terms))

query = "enterprise refund approval after 30 days"
candidates = [
    {"id": "faq", "text": "Refunds are available for standard plans within 30 days.", "rank": 1},
    {"id": "enterprise", "text": "Enterprise refunds after 30 days require finance approval.", "rank": 9},
    {"id": "billing", "text": "Billing invoices are issued monthly.", "rank": 4},
]

reranked = sorted(
    [{**c, "rerank_score": toy_score(query, c["text"])} for c in candidates],
    key=lambda c: c["rerank_score"],
    reverse=True,
)
print([(c["id"], c["rank"], round(c["rerank_score"], 2)) for c in reranked])
blocks.explanation: The toy scorer is intentionally simple; the useful pattern is preserving original rank and final score for inspection.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it, predict which candidate moves above the original rank-1 FAQ.
predictThenReveal.answer: The enterprise chunk rises because it overlaps the specific approval-after-30-days claim. A real reranker should learn richer evidence support than word overlap.

blocks.title: Trace fields
blocks.prompt: Which field helps debug whether reranking hurt a previously good dense result?

options.text: The UI theme used for citations.
Original retrieval rank alongside rerank score and final rank.

blocks.explanation: You need before/after rank data to isolate the reranker’s effect.

modules.title: Release reranking with eval and fallbacks
modules.sub: A reranker changes latency, cost, and answer risk.
modules.summary: Reranking is production-ready when it improves the packed evidence under realistic budgets.
objectives: Measure MRR and packed-context hit rate.
Create fallback behavior for reranker failure.

blocks.title: Reranker wins must survive shipped constraints

spans.text: Evaluate the final context budget, not an offline top-100 leaderboard. The question is whether the answer prompt receives better evidence often enough to justify the latency and cost.
Failure modes include missing candidates, reranker timeouts, stale chunks ranked highly, over-favoring summaries, and degraded exact identifier queries. Route or fallback deliberately.
A reranker outage should degrade to first-stage retrieval with a logged warning, not break every answer.
Use this checklist on answer samples, not only metrics.

items.text: Every generated claim has a citation whose reranked chunk directly supports it.
Queries with exact identifiers still retain exact-match evidence.
Expected sources move into the packed top-k for known failures.
Reranker latency and timeout rates fit the product budget.
Negative or insufficient-evidence cases do not become overconfident answers.

blocks.title: Release decision
blocks.prompt: The reranker improves MRR but doubles p95 latency for simple FAQ lookups. What is a sensible next step?

options.text: Remove retrieval evaluation because MRR improved.
Route reranking to ambiguous or high-risk categories instead of using it everywhere.
Ask the model to answer without citations.

blocks.explanation: Reranking can be selectively applied where the quality gain is worth the cost.

rag.label: RAG
rag.laymanDefinition: Retrieving relevant evidence before generation so answers can be grounded in sources.
rag.technicalNote: RAG quality depends on corpus freshness, chunking, embeddings, filters, ranking, citation handling, and faithfulness evaluation.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.laymanDefinition: A numeric vector representation of text used for semantic comparison.
embedding.technicalNote: Embedding choices fix dimension, distance metric, query/passage formatting, model version, and migration requirements for retrieval.

vector_search.label: Vector search
vector_search.laymanDefinition: Finding nearby vectors to retrieve semantically related chunks.
vector_search.technicalNote: Vector search needs metadata filters, recall tests, index tuning, and fallback for exact terms, IDs, and rare phrases.

chunk.label: Chunk
chunk.laymanDefinition: A source text segment stored and retrieved as a unit.
chunk.technicalNote: Chunk design balances semantic completeness, citation accuracy, token budget, overlap, metadata, and update/delete behavior.

reranker.label: Reranker
reranker.laymanDefinition: A second-stage model or method that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance.
reranker.technicalNote: Rerankers improve top-result precision when candidate recall is adequate, but add latency, cost, and evaluation complexity.

rrf.label: RRF
rrf.laymanDefinition: A rank-fusion method that merges multiple result lists by reciprocal rank.
rrf.technicalNote: RRF is useful for hybrid retrieval because it combines lexical and vector rankings without requiring comparable raw scores.
